issues.legal_issue: A later public-interest writ concerning a common public right is not barred by res judicata when the earlier litigation concerning that right was not bona fide.
material_facts: A later writ sought substantially the same relief concerning the use of public land as an earlier writ.
The earlier court had found that the first petitioner was put forward by a disgruntled builder and that the earlier litigation was not bona fide.
A ground raised in the later writ had not been raised in the earlier writ.
issues.conclusion: The later writ was not barred by res judicata because the earlier litigation was not bona fide, although a matter that might and ought to have been raised earlier may be treated as having been in issue.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Explanation IV treats a matter that might and ought to have been raised in the former suit as having been in issue. Explanation VI applies to litigation bona fide concerning a public right or a private right claimed in common, and binds persons interested in that right; section 91 is relevant to the inclusion of public rights and the prevention of multiplicity of litigation. Section 11 can apply to public-interest litigation, but the prior proceeding must have been bona fide litigation of a common right, rather than a private grievance.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding was a writ brought to pursue a public interest concerning a right common to interested persons.
predicates.prior_litigation_concerned_same_common_r: An earlier proceeding concerned substantially the same common right and sought substantially the same relief.
predicates.prior_litigation_not_bona_fide: The earlier court found that the prior proceeding was not bona fide and had been brought at the instance of a private interested person.

issues.definition: When a public-interest writ concerns a common right previously litigated in a proceeding found not to be bona fide, the later writ is not barred by res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A combined use of land for its designated public purpose and an additional public-purpose use does not amount to a change of user requiring prior modification of the development plan if the designated use is not completely or substantially displaced.
material_facts: The land was reserved for a public transport depot.
The proposed development retained the depot and used part of the land for commercial buildings intended to generate public income.
The court found that the land continued to be substantially used for the designated depot purpose and that the additional use served a public purpose.
issues.conclusion: The combined depot and commercial use did not change the user within the meaning of the regulation, so prior modification of the development plan was not required on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Building Regulation No. 3 requires modification of the development plan before a change of user. The court construed “change,” using its ordinary meanings in the Collins English Dictionary and Oxford Dictionary, as making or becoming different, transforming, or converting; prior modification is necessary where the use is completely or substantially changed. Development Control Rule 3 addresses development conforming to the rules and the use of buildings or premises.

predicates.land_use_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges whether a proposed land use is permitted under applicable planning requirements.
predicates.designated_public_use_continues_substant: The land continues to be substantially used for the public purpose for which it was designated.
predicates.additional_use_does_not_substantially_re: An additional use occupies only part of the land and does not completely or substantially displace the designated use.

issues.definition: When a land-use challenge concerns land that continues substantially to serve its designated public purpose and an additional use does not substantially replace that purpose, the combined use is not treated as a change requiring prior plan modification.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority's development of commercial accommodation in a commercial zone to provide local facilities and support public purposes is within its municipal purposes and is not outside its statutory authority merely because it produces income.
material_facts: The land lay in a commercial zone.
The project retained the public transport depot while providing commercial office accommodation in part of the available space.
The non-refundable premium was earmarked for construction of staff quarters and tenements under a hire-purchase scheme.
The court treated the project as promoting the improvement of the city and providing facilities for the locality.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was not outside the municipality's statutory purposes; providing commercial accommodation in the commercial zone could serve city improvement and public convenience.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 61(t) and 63(k) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act identify city improvement and measures promoting public safety, health, and convenience as municipal functions. Section 87 empowers the Corporation to acquire and hold property for the purposes of the Act. A financial gain does not by itself make a transaction outside those purposes where the use also makes appropriate use of available space and provides facilities consistent with those functions.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_property_transact: The proceeding challenges a municipal authority's transaction involving property it holds.
predicates.property_in_commercial_zone: The property is located in an area designated for commercial activity.
predicates.commercial_facilities_provided_for_local: The municipal authority provides commercial accommodation or related facilities for people in the locality.
predicates.proceeds_earmarked_for_public_purpose: The authority earmarks income from the transaction for a public-purpose project.

issues.definition: When a challenged municipal property transaction provides commercial facilities in a commercial zone and earmarks its proceeds for a public purpose, the transaction falls within municipal purposes.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal property transaction is not shown to be secretive or for grossly inadequate consideration when it is publicly advertised, brought to the attention of builders, and awarded to the bidder offering the higher tender.
material_facts: The authority advertised the opportunity in newspapers and sent notices to numerous builders.
Several builders obtained tender forms, and two tenders were received.
The authority accepted the higher of the two tenders.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was not shown to have been conducted secretly or for wholly inadequate consideration.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the allegation against the established facts concerning publicity and the tender process, including the receipt and comparison of competing offers; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: challenge_to_public_property_transaction and opportunity_publicly_advertised and multiple_builders_notified and competing_tenders_received and higher_tender_accepted

predicates.challenge_to_public_property_transaction: The proceeding alleges that a public authority disposed of or developed public property improperly.
predicates.opportunity_publicly_advertised: The authority publicly advertised the opportunity to interested persons.
predicates.multiple_builders_notified: The authority separately notified multiple potential builders about the opportunity.
predicates.competing_tenders_received: The authority received and compared tenders from more than one bidder.
predicates.higher_tender_accepted: The authority accepted the tender offering more than the competing tender.

issues.definition: When a challenged public-property transaction is publicly advertised, communicated to multiple potential builders, and awarded after competing tenders to the higher bidder, it is not shown to have been secretive or for wholly inadequate consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Official mala fides are not established by a challenge to a municipal transaction when no specific allegation shows that an officer acted with an ulterior or improper motive.
material_facts: The challengers relied on circumstances to allege mala fides in the acceptance of a tender.
No specific allegation was made against an individual officer showing an ulterior or improper motive.
The High Court rejected the allegation for reasons with which the Supreme Court agreed.
issues.conclusion: Mala fides on the part of the municipal officers were not established.
issues.legal_principle: The court evaluated the allegation on the pleadings and circumstances before it and agreed with the High Court's rejection of the claim; it relied on no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_transaction: The proceeding alleges improper conduct by officials in carrying out a municipal transaction.
predicates.no_specific_official_improper_motive_all: The challenger does not specifically allege facts showing that an officer acted with an ulterior or improper motive.

issues.definition: When a municipal transaction is challenged but no specific official improper motive is alleged, official mala fides are not established.
